transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. I'm Santiago. Well, I'm here because... man, it's just been a really frustrating time lately, to be honest with you. I work down at the warehouse, shipping and receiving, you know, mostly checking inventory and dealing with the delivery trucks all day. It's a long shift, and by the time I get home, I'm completely beat. I usually just want to unwind, maybe watch a little TV in the quiet, but then... well, it's the nights that are the real problem. 

I'll be sitting there, and I just start picking at some food. Just a little something at first, you know, to take the edge off the day. But what really worries me, what actually made me finally pick up the phone to make this appointment, is that once I start picking at the food late at night... it's like a switch flips. I'll literally be sitting there, and I tell myself, "That's enough, Santiago. You've had enough." I mean it, too! I know I should stop. But my hand just keeps going back. It's the craziest feeling, like I don't get to make the decision anymore. My brain is saying stop, but my arm is just on autopilot, reaching back for more, and I just can't seem to make myself quit once that starts happening.
Do you feel like you're in control of how much you eat during these late-night episodes?

Yeah, exactly, that's just it. Like I was saying a second ago, there is absolutely zero control. None at all. It's exactly what I meant when I said it's like I don't get to make the decision anymore. 

It's like... well, you know when you're operating machinery? Down at the warehouse, we have these old pallet jacks, and sometimes the brakes just give out. You're pulling the lever, you're telling the machine to stop, but the heavy load just keeps rolling and you just have to stand there and watch it happen. That's exactly what it feels like in my head. I'll be sitting there on my recliner, and my brain is shouting, "That's enough, Santiago. You're done now. Put it away." I hear the words in my own head so clearly, I really do. I'm literally begging myself to stop. 

But my hand? It just completely ignores me. It's like being in the passenger seat of my own body. My hand just dips right back into the bag or the box, over and over, while I'm sitting there watching it happen. It's the most bizarre, frustrating thing in the world because I'm a 48-year-old man, I manage a whole loading dock of guys, I should be able to tell my own arm what to do, right? But in those moments, late at night when the house is quiet and the TV is on... it's like someone else is at the steering wheel. I just don't have a say in it once it starts. The decision is just gone.
Do you feel guilty or ashamed after these late-night eating episodes are over?

Guilty? Oh, man... yeah. That's... that's the worst part of the whole thing, to be honest. It's not just a little guilt, either. It's this heavy, sinking feeling that just settles right in my gut. 

I mean, picture this: it's maybe one or two in the morning. The TV is still going, maybe some infomercial or an old rerun, but I'm not even watching it anymore. I'm just sitting there in my recliner, and the episode—or whatever you want to call it—is finally over. The food is gone, or I've finally managed to pull myself away. And I look down, and there are just... wrappers. Crumbs everywhere. Empty containers sitting on the coffee table. And the silence in the house, it just feels so loud all of a sudden. 

That's when it hits me. The shame is just... it's overwhelming. I'll sit there and think, "Santiago, what is wrong with you? You're a grown man. You run a whole crew at the warehouse. You deal with drivers, you handle invoices, you keep things moving all day long. And you can't even stop yourself from eating a whole box of whatever?" It makes me feel so small, you know? So weak. 

And then I have to clean it all up. That's almost the most humiliating part. I'm gathering up all the evidence, stuffing the wrappers deep down in the trash can so nobody else sees how much I put away. I'm wiping down the table, brushing crumbs off my shirt... and the whole time, I'm just beating myself up. I tell myself I'm never going to do it again. I swear to myself, "Tomorrow night is going to be different. I'm just going to have dinner and that's it." But then I wake up the next morning, and I still feel that hangover of guilt, just dragging me down before I even clock in for my shift. It's exhausting, doc. It really is. It just makes me feel like I'm completely broken.
Do you feel like you're eating quickly during these late-night episodes?

Yeah, I do. It's... it's not like a normal meal, that's for sure. 

When I sit down with my sister and her kids for Sunday dinner, you know, we take our time. We talk about the week, we pass the dishes around, we actually enjoy the roast or the enchiladas or whatever she made. You chew, you swallow, you take a sip of water, you laugh at a joke. It's an event. It takes an hour, maybe more. 

But this? These nights in the recliner? It's nothing like that. It's... man, it's almost frantic. I'm just shoveling it in. I don't even know if I'm chewing half the time. It's like I'm in some kind of race, but I'm the only one running. I'll have a bag of chips or a sleeve of cookies, and I'm just pulling them out and putting them away so fast. It's almost like... like I'm trying to get it all done and over with before anyone in the house wakes up and catches me, even though I live alone right now. But it's that same feeling, that rushed, secretive panic. 

And the crazy part is, I don't even really taste it. You'd think if I'm eating a whole row of Oreos, I'd at least be enjoying the chocolate, right? But I'm going so fast, just one after the other, boom, boom, boom. The flavor barely even registers on my tongue before I'm swallowing and reaching for the next one. It's just about getting it in, getting that feeling, whatever that feeling is. Sometimes I'll look down and the bag is half empty, and I'll think, "Wait, did I even taste those?" And the answer is usually no. It's just a blur of motion. Hand to mouth, hand to mouth, as fast as I can go.
Do these late-night eating episodes happen at the same time every day or night?

Well, it is not like I have an alarm set for it, you know? It is not like punching in at the warehouse where it happens at exactly eleven on the dot every single night. But there is definitely a pattern to it if I really sit down and think about it. If I look back over, say, the past several months... yeah, for the past several months, it has been happening most weeks at least once. Sometimes it might just be that one time, but it is pretty consistent week to week. 

And it almost always lines up with a specific kind of situation rather than a specific time on the clock. It is usually on a night when there are plenty of leftovers sitting in the fridge. Like, maybe my sister came over and brought a huge tray of baked ziti, or I had some of the guys from the loading dock over to watch the game and we ordered way too much pizza and wings. There will be all these extra boxes and Tupperware containers just sitting in there. And it always happens after everyone else has gone to bed. 

I know I mentioned earlier that I live alone, but I have family over a lot, or my buddies will crash on the couch after a late game. So it is always when they finally go to sleep, or when they finally head home and the house gets completely, totally quiet. That is the real danger zone for me. It is like the second the coast is clear and I know nobody is going to walk into the kitchen and catch me... that is when the urge really hits. Just me, the quiet house, and a fridge full of food that nobody is really keeping track of. I will just sit there in my recliner thinking about those leftovers, knowing they are just a few steps away in the kitchen, until I finally give in. So yeah, not a specific time, but definitely a specific type of night.
Do you ever find that you've eaten something during one of these episodes and then later can't remember eating it?

Well... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I remember it. It's not like I'm sleepwalking or blacking out or anything like that. I know exactly what I'm doing, and I know exactly what I'm eating. 

I mean, I might not be tasting it, like I was saying before, because I'm going so fast. And sometimes, yeah, I'll look at the empty boxes the next morning and think, "Man, did I really eat all of that?" But it's not because I literally forgot doing it. It's more just... disbelief, I guess? Like, I remember being there in the kitchen, pulling out the Tupperware of ziti, grabbing a fork, not even bothering to heat it up or put it on a plate. I remember standing there in the glow of the fridge light, just shoveling it in. I remember the cold cheese, the sauce. I remember moving on to the leftover garlic bread. I remember all of it. 

So it's not a memory issue. It's just... it's almost like I'm watching myself do it, knowing I shouldn't, but I can't stop. But the memory is there. Clear as day. Unfortunately. Because if I could forget it, maybe the guilt wouldn't be so bad the next morning, you know? But I remember every single bite, even if it was just a blur when it was happening. So, no, I don't forget. I wish I did, sometimes, but I don't.
Do you ever find yourself eating a large amount of food in a short period of time during the day, not just at night?

Well, during the day... if you mean right in the middle of the afternoon, no, not usually. Because I'm at the warehouse, you know? I'm checking inventory, running the forklift, trying to hear myself think over the backup alarms. You can't exactly stop to eat a massive meal when there's an eighteen-wheeler waiting at dock four to be unloaded and the driver is tapping his watch. I just don't have the time or the privacy for it there. 

But... if you mean outside of those late-night hours I was telling you about, like right after my shift ends in the early evening? Yeah. Yeah, that definitely happens. 

I'll get home from work, and I'm just exhausted, right? My feet are aching from standing on those concrete floors all day. I'll walk in, and I'll tell myself I'm just going to grab a quick bite before I hit the shower. Just a little something to take the edge off. But then... well, on some nights after work, I can go through an unbelievable amount of food. I can go through several tamales, a big bowl of pozole, a whole stack of tortillas, and whatever rice or beans are left in the fridge from the weekend. 

And the crazy thing is, I don't even sit down at the table to do it. I'll do it all while standing right there in the kitchen, still in my heavy work boots, leaning against the counter. I always try to convince myself in the moment that I'm just, I don't know, being practical? Like I'm just cleaning up leftovers so they don't go bad, or so I can finally wash the containers and clear out some fridge space. I'll think, "Oh, the rice is going to dry out by tomorrow, I should just finish it." 

But I'm not just having a bite. I'm eating enough for three grown men, and I'm doing it in like ten or fifteen minutes. Just standing there, going from the tamales to the pozole to the beans, barely taking a breath, acting like I'm doing a chore by clearing out the fridge. So, yeah, it's not always pitch black outside when it happens. Sometimes the sun is still going down, and I haven't even taken my work jacket off yet.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?

Well, honestly... no, not really. I mean, I don't think so. It's kind of hard to say for sure because I don't actually own a scale anymore. I used to have one of those old dial ones in the bathroom, but the spring got totally busted the last time I moved, which was, oh, probably five or six years ago now. I just never bothered to go to the store and buy a new one. 

And as for my clothes... I wear these heavy canvas work pants at the warehouse, the kind with the reinforced knees because I'm always scraping up against wooden pallets and cardboard crates out on the dock. They're pretty baggy to begin with, and they just kind of wear out and stretch over time, so I can't really use my belt loop as a measuring stick, you know? It's not like I'm putting on a tailored suit every morning where I'd feel every little pinch.

You would think I'd be gaining, though, right? With all those late-night leftovers and the tamales I was just telling you about, you'd think I'd be ballooning up, putting on ten pounds a week. But it hasn't been like that. I mean, I definitely have a gut, I'm a big guy, but it hasn't been some sudden, massive change over these past few months. It's just sort of... steady. 

Plus, my sister hasn't said anything, and trust me, she is always the very first person to point out if I'm looking heavier. She's got absolutely no filter, none at all. If she thought my face was getting rounder, she'd poke my cheek right in front of everybody and tell me to lay off the beer—even though, like I said, it's not the beer doing it, it's the food. But she hasn't said a peep about my size lately. So I figure I must be burning just enough off walking miles on those concrete floors all day, climbing on and off the forklift, sweating in the warehouse, to kind of keep things level. So, yeah, no big changes in my weight that I've noticed.
Do you ever feel like you're unable to control how much you eat during meals or snacks at other times of the day, not just at night?

Well, for regular meals, like if I'm just having lunch on my break at the warehouse? No, not at all. I'll sit down in the breakroom with the guys, eat my turkey sandwich, maybe have a bag of chips, and when my thirty minutes are up, I toss the wrapper in the trash and go back out to the floor. I'm completely in the driver's seat then. Same thing if I'm at my sister's place for a Sunday cookout. I'll have a plate, I eat a normal amount, and I stop. 

But... it's those other times. The times when I'm alone in the house. What worries me is that once I start picking at the food late at night, it's a whole different story. I'll be standing there in the kitchen, and I tell myself, "That's enough, Santiago. You don't need any more, you're going to feel like garbage tomorrow." I mean, I literally say it to myself in my head. But my hand keeps going back like I don't get to make the decision anymore. 

It's the most frustrating thing in the world, doc. It's like my brain is completely disconnected from my arm. I'll be looking right at the container of food, knowing I should just snap the lid back on and go to bed because I have to be up at 5 AM to open the loading dock. But my hand just reaches out, grabs another bite, and brings it to my mouth. Over and over. During the day, I'm the one in charge, right? I steer the forklift, I manage the inventory, I tell my body what to do. But at night, once I start picking at those leftovers... I just lose all say in the matter. It's like someone else takes over the controls, and I'm just trapped there watching it happen. So, yeah, during the day I'm fine, but at night, the control is just gone.
Do you feel guilty or ashamed after eating a large amount of food during the day, like when you're standing in the kitchen after work?

Guilty? Ashamed? You know, I... I don't really know if I'd use those words for when it happens right after work. I'm not entirely sure. Because, see, when I get home at that time, like I was saying, I'm just so completely drained. The drive back from the warehouse is always a total nightmare—bumper-to-bumper traffic, everyone cutting each other off, and I've already been dealing with impatient truck drivers all day, so my patience is completely shot by the time I pull into my driveway. 

So I walk in, I drop my keys in that little ceramic bowl by the door, and then the eating happens. And right after I finish—after I've stood there and cleared out all those leftovers, the tamales, the rice, everything—it's not like I'm standing there beating myself up about it. I don't think I even have the energy left in my body to feel something as heavy as shame right then. 

Mostly, I just feel... well, physically heavy. Just stuffed. My stomach is stretched out, my feet are still throbbing from the concrete floors, and my brain is just kind of buzzing like static. I'll look at the empty containers, and maybe I feel a little, I don't know, annoyed with myself? Like, "Well, that was stupid, Santiago, now you have to go buy more groceries this weekend." But it's not this deep, dark guilt. 

I just take the empty Tupperware—you know, the plastic ones that always get those orange grease stains from the pozole that never really wash out no matter how hard you scrub them with the sponge—and I toss them in the sink. Then I finally unlace my work boots, peel off my socks, and go take my shower. Honestly, the hot water is usually the only thing I'm looking forward to all afternoon anyway. 

So, yeah, I wouldn't say I feel ashamed in that specific moment. I haven't really noticed feeling that way right after my shift. It's more just... being full, and being tired, and just wanting to finally get off my feet and turn my brain off for the night.
Do you feel guilty or ashamed after eating a large amount of food during the day, outside of your late-night episodes?

Well, no, not really. Because, see, during the actual day... I don't really eat a large amount of food to begin with. Like I was saying before about my lunch breaks, my day at the warehouse is just so completely scheduled out. From the minute I clock in at 5:30 AM, it's just go, go, go. 

We get exactly thirty minutes for lunch at noon, and they are strict about it. And honestly, doc, by the time you walk all the way from the loading dock—which is way down at the south end of the building—and wait in line at the wash station to scrub the dirt and cardboard dust off your hands with that gritty orange pumice soap they keep in the dispensers... you're left with maybe twenty minutes to actually sit down. 

So I just sit at this wobbly folding table in the breakroom with a couple of the other guys, usually Hector and Dave, and I just eat my regular turkey sandwich or whatever small thing I brought. There's just no opportunity to eat a huge amount of food. You couldn't even if you wanted to, because the foreman is always walking by with his clipboard, tapping his watch and making sure nobody is lingering when the buzzer goes off. 

Because of all that, I'm just eating a normal, quick meal, so there's absolutely nothing to feel guilty or ashamed about. I don't even have time to think about it, I'm just fueling up so I don't pass out when I get back on the forklift. It's really only when I'm totally alone in my house, with no schedule and no one around, that the eating gets out of hand. But during the daylight hours, outside of the house? No, I don't feel any shame or guilt because I'm just doing what everyone else is doing.
Do you usually eat more when you're feeling stressed, anxious, or upset?

Stressed? Anxious? You know, I've thought about that, because you always hear about people doing that on TV—you know, eating a whole carton of ice cream because they had a bad day or they're crying about something. But for me? No, I really don't think so. I haven't noticed a connection like that at all. 

Because, see, when I'm actually stressed out... like, really stressed? My stomach just completely ties itself up into a tight little knot. Like last month, for example, we had our quarterly inventory audit down at the warehouse. Absolute nightmare. The new handheld barcode scanners they gave us weren't syncing up with the main computer database, we had three entire pallets of industrial solvent that completely vanished from the system, and the regional manager is pacing around the floor with this scowl on his face, just looking for someone to blame. That is stress, doc. My heart was pounding, I was sweating right through my uniform shirt, and I was so anxious about getting written up that I couldn't even look at food. Hector offered me half of his meatball sub because I worked right through my lunch break trying to manually reconcile the shipping manifests, and I just waved him off. The thought of eating when I'm worked up like that actually makes me feel a little nauseous. I just drink that terrible breakroom coffee—the stuff that's been sitting on the burner since 6 AM and tastes like burnt pennies—and I keep my head down.

And even if it's not work, like if I'm upset about something personal? Say my ex-wife calls and starts getting on my case about helping pay for our daughter's car repairs, and we get into a whole shouting match over the phone. When I finally hang up, I'm furious, sure. I'm pacing the living room, my blood is boiling. But I don't go straight to the fridge. I'll go out to the garage, maybe organize my socket wrenches, or just sit out on the back porch in the dark and try to cool off. 

The times when I do end up eating all that food late at night... I'm not really upset or anxious when it happens. It's just quiet. The house is totally silent, the TV is usually off. I'm not mad at anyone, I'm not worried about the forklift breaking down, I'm just... there. So, no, I wouldn't say stress or feeling upset is what triggers the eating. If anything, being stressed makes me skip eating entirely.
Do these episodes of eating large amounts of food happen regularly, like on a weekly basis?

Regularly? Yeah, I suppose it is pretty regular if you look at it on a calendar. I mean, I never really kept a log of it or anything, but... yeah, if I sit down and really think about it, for the past several months, it’s been happening most weeks at least once. 

It kind of started getting into this pattern a while back, maybe around the time the weather started turning and we started getting slammed at the warehouse with the seasonal shipments. You just get into this exhausting rut, you know? But yeah, at least once a week, for sure. 

And it’s almost always on a night when there are plenty of leftovers just sitting right there in the fridge. Like, for instance, on a Sunday I might decide to cook up a massive pot of chili or a huge tray of chicken enchiladas. I do that because I figure, hey, I can pack this up in my cooler and take it to work for lunch all week. It makes sense, right? It saves money, keeps me away from the overpriced vending machines in the breakroom. So I'll have all these containers stacked up on the middle shelf of the fridge, just waiting there. 

But then... well, then a Tuesday or Wednesday night rolls around. And it always happens late. It's usually on a night when everyone else has gone to bed. Like if my daughter is staying over for the week, or if my brother is crashing in the spare room while he looks for a new apartment. Once they finally turn in and shut their doors, the whole house just gets incredibly still. The TV is off, the street outside is quiet, and it feels exactly like I was saying before—like I'm completely alone in the house with no one around. 

It's just me awake in the dark, and I know all that food is just sitting in there, and... I don't know, I just end up eating it. But yeah, to answer your question, it's definitely been a weekly thing for the last few months now.
Do you think your late-night eating episodes are triggered by any specific emotions, such as boredom, sadness, or loneliness?

Boredom, sadness, loneliness... you know, I've really tried to put my finger on exactly what's going through my head when I'm standing there in front of the open fridge, but honestly? I don't really think it's any of those things. 

Take sadness, for example. I know what sadness feels like. When my dad passed away back in '14, or when the divorce was finalizing and I had to pack up half my life into those cardboard U-Haul boxes while my ex-wife watched from the kitchen... that was sadness. I felt heavy, you know? Like I couldn't get out of bed. But when I'm up at 1 AM eating cold chili out of a Tupperware container, I'm not sad. I'm not crying or feeling sorry for myself at all. 

And loneliness... I mean, sure, like I was saying before, the house is completely empty, or everyone's asleep and their doors are shut. But I've always been a bit of a night owl, ever since I was a kid, really. I actually kind of like the quiet after a long day at the warehouse with all the forklifts beeping and the radios blaring. I don't feel lonely when I'm the only one awake. I'm just... awake. 

As for boredom, well, if you saw my house, you'd know I have a list of chores a mile long. If I was just bored, I could go out to the garage and finish sanding down that old oak coffee table I found at the flea market last month. I've got a whole stack of sandpaper out there—120 grit, 220 grit—just sitting on the workbench waiting for me to get to it. Or I could turn on the TV and watch one of those World War II documentaries on the History Channel. I've got a whole backlog of them recorded on the DVR. So it's not like I don't have plenty of things I could be doing to occupy my time if I was just looking for entertainment. 

It's more just like... my brain just kind of goes completely blank. I'm not trying to fix a bad mood or fill some emotional void or anything dramatic like you see in the movies. I'm not feeling much of anything at all. I just sort of wander into the kitchen, the light from the fridge comes on, and... I don't know, it just happens. There really aren't any big feelings attached to it, if that makes any sense.
Do you think you would be able to stop eating once you start if you really wanted to?

Stop? Man, that’s... that’s the million-dollar question, isn’t it? Because you’d think so. You’d think a grown man, 48 years old, who manages an entire warehouse floor and keeps track of thousands of SKUs every single day, could just put a lid back on a piece of plastic Tupperware and walk away. I mean, it sounds so simple when you say it out loud. Just stop eating. Just close the fridge door. 

But... and this is the part that actually worries me, to be completely honest with you. What worries me is that once I start picking at the food late at night, I literally have this whole conversation with myself in my head. I’ll be standing there in the kitchen, just the light from the refrigerator shining on me, and I’ll look down and see that I’ve already eaten half of my lunches for the rest of the week, and I tell myself, "That's enough, Santiago. Put the fork down. Snap the lid back on and go to bed." I say it just like that, clear as day. 

But then... it’s the strangest thing, doc. My hand just keeps going back. It’s like my arm has a mind of its own, just scooping up another bite, and then another bite, even while my brain is actively telling me to quit. It honestly feels like I don't get to make the decision anymore. 

I’ll even try to physically step back from the counter, you know? Like, I'll take a step back onto the linoleum, wipe my mouth, maybe turn to go rinse the fork off in the sink. But before the water even gets warm, I’m turning right back around to the fridge. It makes absolutely no sense. I want to stop, I really do, because I know I’m gonna be so annoyed the next day when I have to go buy a twelve-dollar turkey sandwich at the deli next to the warehouse because I ate all my meal prep. But in that exact moment, at one or two in the morning... no. I really don't think I can stop. It’s just... the hand keeps moving, no matter what I tell myself.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you start, even if you want to?

Yeah, exactly. Like I was just saying a second ago, that's really the crux of it. I know I kind of just went on a whole tangent about it, but... yeah, it's exactly that. I am just unable to stop. 

And I want to make sure I'm explaining it right, because honestly, what worries me is that once I start picking at the food late at night, I am fully aware of what's happening. It's not like I'm sleepwalking or in some kind of trance. I literally tell myself, right there in my own head, "That's enough, Santiago. You've had enough, wrap it up." I try to reason with myself the exact same way I'd reason with one of the new forklift drivers on the loading dock who's rushing and messing up a pallet stack. I give myself a direct order to just walk away. 

But... my hand just keeps going back. It keeps scooping up another bite, and then another. It’s like my hand and my brain are completely disconnected from each other. I’ll be staring right at the container, knowing I need that food for my shift tomorrow, knowing I'm going to be mad at myself in the morning, but the fork just keeps moving. 

It really does feel like I don't get to make the decision anymore. It’s a total loss of the steering wheel, you know? Like the brakes are just completely gone. I want to stop, I'm actively telling myself to stop, but the physical action just overrides everything else. It's incredibly frustrating, doc, it really is, because I've always prided myself on being a disciplined guy with my inventory logs and my work schedule, but standing there at the counter... I just can't stop.
Do you think your eating episodes are ever triggered by feelings of emptiness or emotional numbness?

Emptiness? Emotional numbness? Hmm. You know, when you use words like that, it makes it sound like... like I'm walking around with this big, gaping hole in my chest, or like I'm totally checked out of my own life. And I really don't think that's it at all. 

I mean, take the warehouse, for example. When we have an empty bay on the floor—say, aisle four, section B—and there are no pallets there... it's just empty. It's just space waiting for the next shipment of auto parts or whatever we're unloading from the trucks that week. It's not a bad thing, it's just a fact of the inventory. But when people talk about emotional emptiness, it always sounds so heavy, you know? Like you're missing a piece of your soul or something dramatic. I don't feel like that. I really don't. I have a good life. I've got a job that keeps me on my toes, I've got guys on the floor who rely on me to make sure the shift runs smooth, I pay my bills on time. I don't feel empty inside. 

And numbness... I mean, what does that even mean, really? Like when you go to the dentist and they shoot your gums full of Novocain to fill a cavity, and you can't feel your own lip for four hours? Or do you mean numb like I just don't care about anything? Because I definitely care. I care a lot. If one of my forklift drivers comes in late, I care. If the inventory logs don't match the physical count at the end of the month, I care—probably too much, honestly, I'll spend three hours tracking down a single missing barcode just to make sure the books are perfect. I'm definitely not walking around like a zombie.

So, no, I wouldn't say I feel numb, and I wouldn't say I feel empty. When I'm standing there in the kitchen at two in the morning... I know I said earlier that my brain goes blank, but it's not because I'm emotionally numb. It's not like I'm trying to stuff food into some deep emotional void to make myself feel alive again. It's just... I'm just standing there, and the eating just starts. I'm not trying to fix anything or run away from any deep, dark feelings of emptiness. I know it probably makes your job harder that I don't have some big psychological reason for it, like you'd read about in a textbook, but I really just don't see it being about feeling empty. It's just me, the fridge, and a complete lack of brakes.
Do you feel like you have control over what you eat during regular meals?

Oh, absolutely. Regular meals? I have total control. It's actually a night and day difference, doc. 

Like, take my mornings, for example. I'm up at 5:15 AM every single day without fail. I make my coffee—black, no sugar, because I don't want to deal with a sugar crash later when I'm trying to reconcile the shipping manifests—and I make exactly two eggs. Maybe one piece of whole wheat toast. I sit at my little kitchen table, I eat my breakfast, I wash the plate, put it in the drying rack, and I head out the door. It's completely routine. I never sit there feeling like I need to scramble a third egg, or like I'm going to suddenly eat the entire loaf of bread. I just eat what I made, and I'm good.

And then at work, it's the exact same story. We have our lunch whistle at 12:30 PM. Usually, I'll check the loading dock first, just to make sure the afternoon delivery trucks are lined up right, because if I don't keep an eye on them, the new drivers will back in crooked and block bay three. But after I sort that out, I head into the break room, I open up my cooler, and I take out whatever meal prep I brought for the day. Chicken, rice, some green beans, whatever it is. I sit with the guys, we talk about the football game or complain about the regional manager, I finish my Tupperware, and that's it. I'm done. I don't go hunting for quarters for the vending machine, I don't go poking around the communal fridge to see if somebody left a donut in there. I just pack up my bag, wash my fork, and go right back out to the floor. 

Even dinner is usually totally fine. I get home around six, I'm tired, my feet ache from standing on concrete all day, so I'll cook up a pork chop or heat up some soup, sit in my recliner, watch a little TV, and that's that. 

During the day, from 5 AM until maybe 9 or 10 at night, I am completely in the driver's seat. I decide what goes on the plate, I eat it, and I move on with my life. There's no weird pull, no fighting with myself. I plan it out and I execute it, just like I manage the warehouse inventory. So yeah, when it comes to normal, regular meals, I have zero problems. I'm completely in control. That's why the late-night stuff makes me so mad, because I know I have the discipline during the day! It just all goes out the window later on.
Do you ever eat until you feel uncomfortably full during these episodes?

Uncomfortably full... yeah. Yeah, that's putting it mildly, doc. It’s like... well, you know when you’re loading a pallet and you try to squeeze just one more row of boxes on top, even though the shrink wrap is already stretching to its absolute limit? That’s what it feels like. 

By the time I finally snap out of it and actually stop eating, my stomach just feels so incredibly tight. Tight and heavy, like I swallowed a cinder block. It's not just the "oh, I had a big Thanksgiving dinner" kind of full where you want to take a nice nap. It's a genuinely bad physical feeling. I'll put whatever container is left in the sink—or the trash, if I finished the whole thing, which happens more often than I want to admit—and I can't even walk straight back to my bedroom. 

I end up having to go into the living room and just sit on the edge of the couch for a while. I can't lean back, I can't bend over... like, if I dropped the TV remote, I couldn't even bend over to pick it up because bending over just feels so bad. And lying down? Forget about it. Lying down is completely out of the question because it makes the pressure so much worse, like all that heavy food is pushing right up into my chest. 

So I just sit there on the very edge of the cushions, kind of staring at the floor, waiting for it to settle down enough so I can finally go lay in bed. And sitting there, in the quiet, feeling like my stomach is about to split open... that's when it really hits me how much I messed up. Because I know I have to be up at 5:15, like I told you, and I'm sitting there at 2:30 in the morning, physically miserable, just waiting for gravity to do its job so I don't feel sick when I lay flat. It's a terrible routine, it really is. It just ruins the whole next morning because I wake up still feeling sluggish and heavy from it all, before I even step foot on the warehouse floor.

patient.answer:
Hi, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. I'm Santiago. Well, I'm here because... man, it's just been a really frustrating time lately, to be honest with you. I work down at the warehouse, shipping and receiving, you know, mostly checking inventory and dealing with the delivery trucks all day. It's a long shift, and by the time I get home, I'm completely beat. I usually just want to unwind, maybe watch a little TV in the quiet, but then... well, it's the nights that are the real problem. 

I'll be sitting there, and I just start picking at some food. Just a little something at first, you know, to take the edge off the day. But what really worries me, what actually made me finally pick up the phone to make this appointment, is that once I start picking at the food late at night... it's like a switch flips. I'll literally be sitting there, and I tell myself, "That's enough, Santiago. You've had enough." I mean it, too! I know I should stop. But my hand just keeps going back. It's the craziest feeling, like I don't get to make the decision anymore. My brain is saying stop, but my arm is just on autopilot, reaching back for more, and I just can't seem to make myself quit once that starts happening.

patient.answer:
Yeah, exactly, that's just it. Like I was saying a second ago, there is absolutely zero control. None at all. It's exactly what I meant when I said it's like I don't get to make the decision anymore. 

It's like... well, you know when you're operating machinery? Down at the warehouse, we have these old pallet jacks, and sometimes the brakes just give out. You're pulling the lever, you're telling the machine to stop, but the heavy load just keeps rolling and you just have to stand there and watch it happen. That's exactly what it feels like in my head. I'll be sitting there on my recliner, and my brain is shouting, "That's enough, Santiago. You're done now. Put it away." I hear the words in my own head so clearly, I really do. I'm literally begging myself to stop. 

But my hand? It just completely ignores me. It's like being in the passenger seat of my own body. My hand just dips right back into the bag or the box, over and over, while I'm sitting there watching it happen. The decision is just gone.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Oh, man... yeah. That's... that's the worst part of the whole thing, to be honest. It's not just a little guilt, either. It's this heavy, sinking feeling that just settles right in my gut. 

I mean, picture this: it's maybe one or two in the morning. The TV is still going, maybe some infomercial or an old rerun, but I'm not even watching it anymore. I'm just sitting there in my recliner, and the episode—or whatever you want to call it—is finally over. The food is gone, or I've finally managed to pull myself away. And I look down, and there are just... wrappers. Crumbs everywhere. Empty containers sitting on the coffee table. And the silence in the house, it just feels so loud all of a sudden. 

That's when it hits me. The shame is just... it's overwhelming. I'll sit there and think, "Santiago, what is wrong with you? You're a grown man. You run a whole crew at the warehouse. You deal with drivers, you handle invoices, you keep things moving all day long. And you can't even stop yourself from eating a whole box of whatever?" It makes me feel so small, you know? So weak. 

And then I have to clean it all up. That's almost the most humiliating part. I'm gathering up all the evidence, stuffing the wrappers deep down in the trash can so nobody else sees how much I put away. I'm wiping down the table, brushing crumbs off my shirt... and the whole time, I'm just beating myself up. I tell myself I'm never going to do it again. I swear to myself, "Tomorrow night is going to be different. I'm just going to have dinner and that's it." But then I wake up the next morning, and I still feel that hangover of guilt, just dragging me down before I even clock in for my shift. It's exhausting, doc. It really is. It just makes me feel like I'm completely broken.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's late-night eating episodes are accompanied by a sense of eating rapidly

target_item.name: Rapid_Eating
target_item.manifestation: I eat it fast, not like when I'm sitting with family, but more like I'm trying to get it done before anyone wakes up, barely tasting the food.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks if the patient feels they are eating quickly during their late-night episodes, which maps to the Rapid_Eating symptom.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I do. It's... it's not like a normal meal, that's for sure. 

When I sit down with my sister and her kids for Sunday dinner, you know, we take our time. We talk about the week, we pass the dishes around, we actually enjoy the roast or the enchiladas or whatever she made. You chew, you swallow, you take a sip of water, you laugh at a joke. It's an event. It takes an hour, maybe more. 

But this? These nights in the recliner? It's nothing like that. It's... man, it's almost frantic. I'm just shoveling it in. I don't even know if I'm chewing half the time. It's like I'm in some kind of race, but I'm the only one running. I'll have a bag of chips or a sleeve of cookies, and I'm just pulling them out and putting them away so fast. It's almost like... like I'm trying to get it all done and over with before anyone in the house wakes up and catches me, even though I live alone right now. But it's that same feeling, that rushed, secretive panic. 

And the crazy part is, I don't even really taste it. You'd think if I'm eating a whole row of Oreos, I'd at least be enjoying the chocolate, right? But I'm going so fast, just one after the other, boom, boom, boom. The flavor barely even registers on my tongue before I'm swallowing and reaching for the next one. It's just about getting it in, getting that feeling, whatever that feeling is. Sometimes I'll look down and the bag is half empty, and I'll think, "Wait, did I even taste those?" And the answer is usually no. It's just a blur of motion. Hand to mouth, hand to mouth, as fast as I can go.

doctor.question: Do these late-night eating episodes happen at the same time every day or night?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1

patient.answer:
Well, it is not like I have an alarm set for it, you know? It is not like punching in at the warehouse where it happens at exactly eleven on the dot every single night. But there is definitely a pattern to it if I really sit down and think about it. If I look back over, say, the past several months... yeah, for the past several months, it has been happening most weeks at least once. Sometimes it might just be that one time, but it is pretty consistent week to week. 

And it almost always lines up with a specific kind of situation rather than a specific time on the clock. It is usually on a night when there are plenty of leftovers sitting in the fridge. Like, maybe my sister came over and brought a huge tray of baked ziti, or I had some of the guys from the loading dock over to watch the game and we ordered way too much pizza and wings. There will be all these extra boxes and Tupperware containers just sitting in there. And it always happens after everyone else has gone to bed. 

I know I mentioned earlier that I live alone, but I have family over a lot, or my buddies will crash on the couch after a late game. So it is always when they finally go to sleep, or when they finally head home and the house gets completely, totally quiet. That is the real danger zone for me. It is like the second the coast is clear and I know nobody is going to walk into the kitchen and catch me... that is when the urge really hits. Just me, the quiet house, and a fridge full of food that nobody is really keeping track of. I will just sit there in my recliner thinking about those leftovers, knowing they are just a few steps away in the kitchen, until I finally give in. So yeah, not a specific time, but definitely a specific type of night.

patient.answer:
Well... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I remember it. It's not like I'm sleepwalking or blacking out or anything like that. I know exactly what I'm doing, and I know exactly what I'm eating. 

I mean, I might not be tasting it, like I was saying before, because I'm going so fast. And sometimes, yeah, I'll look at the empty boxes the next morning and think, "Man, did I really eat all of that?" But it's not because I literally forgot doing it. It's more just... disbelief, I guess? Like, I remember being there in the kitchen, pulling out the Tupperware of ziti, grabbing a fork, not even bothering to heat it up or put it on a plate. I remember standing there in the glow of the fridge light, just shoveling it in. I remember the cold cheese, the sauce. I remember moving on to the leftover garlic bread. I remember all of it. 

So it's not a memory issue. It's just... it's almost like I'm watching myself do it, knowing I shouldn't, but I can't stop. But the memory is there. Clear as day. Unfortunately. Because if I could forget it, maybe the guilt wouldn't be so bad the next morning, you know? But I remember every single bite, even if it was just a blur when it was happening. So, no, I don't forget. I wish I did, sometimes, but I don't.

patient.answer:
Well, during the day... if you mean right in the middle of the afternoon, no, not usually. Because I'm at the warehouse, you know? I'm checking inventory, running the forklift, trying to hear myself think over the backup alarms. You can't exactly stop to eat a massive meal when there's an eighteen-wheeler waiting at dock four to be unloaded and the driver is tapping his watch. I just don't have the time or the privacy for it there. 

But... if you mean outside of those late-night hours I was telling you about, like right after my shift ends in the early evening? Yeah. Yeah, that definitely happens. 

I'll get home from work, and I'm just exhausted, right? My feet are aching from standing on those concrete floors all day. I'll walk in, and I'll tell myself I'm just going to grab a quick bite before I hit the shower. Just a little something to take the edge off. But then... well, on some nights after work, I can go through an unbelievable amount of food. I can go through several tamales, a big bowl of pozole, a whole stack of tortillas, and whatever rice or beans are left in the fridge from the weekend. 

And the crazy thing is, I don't even sit down at the table to do it. I'll do it all while standing right there in the kitchen, still in my heavy work boots, leaning against the counter. I always try to convince myself in the moment that I'm just, I don't know, being practical? Like I'm just cleaning up leftovers so they don't go bad, or so I can finally wash the containers and clear out some fridge space. I'll think, "Oh, the rice is going to dry out by tomorrow, I should just finish it." 

But I'm not just having a bite. I'm eating enough for three grown men, and I'm doing it in like ten or fifteen minutes. Just standing there, going from the tamales to the pozole to the beans, barely taking a breath, acting like I'm doing a chore by clearing out the fridge. So, yeah, it's not always pitch black outside when it happens. Sometimes the sun is still going down, and I haven't even taken my work jacket off yet.

patient.answer:
Well, honestly... no, not really. I mean, I don't think so. It's kind of hard to say for sure because I don't actually own a scale anymore. I used to have one of those old dial ones in the bathroom, but the spring got totally busted the last time I moved, which was, oh, probably five or six years ago now. I just never bothered to go to the store and buy a new one. 

And as for my clothes... I wear these heavy canvas work pants at the warehouse, the kind with the reinforced knees because I'm always scraping up against wooden pallets and cardboard crates out on the dock. They're pretty baggy to begin with, and they just kind of wear out and stretch over time, so I can't really use my belt loop as a measuring stick, you know? It's not like I'm putting on a tailored suit every morning where I'd feel every little pinch.

You would think I'd be gaining, though, right? With all those late-night leftovers and the tamales I was just telling you about, you'd think I'd be ballooning up, putting on ten pounds a week. But it hasn't been like that. I mean, I definitely have a gut, I'm a big guy, but it hasn't been some sudden, massive change over these past few months. It's just sort of... steady. 

Plus, my sister hasn't said anything, and trust me, she is always the very first person to point out if I'm looking heavier. She's got absolutely no filter, none at all. If she thought my face was getting rounder, she'd poke my cheek right in front of everybody and tell me to lay off the beer—even though, like I said, it's not the beer doing it, it's the food. But she hasn't said a peep about my size lately. So I figure I must be burning just enough off walking miles on those concrete floors all day, climbing on and off the forklift, sweating in the warehouse, to kind of keep things level. So, yeah, no big changes in my weight that I've noticed.

I'm completely in the driver's seat then. Same thing if I'm at my sister's place for a Sunday cookout. I'll have a plate, I eat a normal amount, and I stop.

It's the most frustrating thing in the world, doc. It's like my brain is completely disconnected from my arm. But my hand just reaches out, grabs another bite, and brings it to my mouth. Over and over. During the day, I'm the one in charge, right? I steer the forklift, I manage the inventory, I tell my body what to do. But at night, once I start picking at those leftovers... I just lose all say in the matter. It's like someone else takes over the controls, and I'm just trapped there watching it happen. So, yeah, during the day I'm fine, but at night, the control is just gone.

doctor.intent: determine if patient experiences feelings of guilt or shame after daytime eating episodes
doctor.question: Do you feel guilty or ashamed after eating a large amount of food during the day, like when you're standing in the kitchen after work?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling guilty or ashamed after a binge eating episode (which corresponds to the DSM-5 criterion of feeling disgusted, depressed, or very guilty afterward). This specific symptom is not included in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Ashamed? You know, I... I don't really know if I'd use those words for when it happens right after work. I'm not entirely sure. Because, see, when I get home at that time, like I was saying, I'm just so completely drained. The drive back from the warehouse is always a total nightmare—bumper-to-bumper traffic, everyone cutting each other off, and I've already been dealing with impatient truck drivers all day, so my patience is completely shot by the time I pull into my driveway. 

So I walk in, I drop my keys in that little ceramic bowl by the door, and then the eating happens. And right after I finish—after I've stood there and cleared out all those leftovers, the tamales, the rice, everything—it's not like I'm standing there beating myself up about it. I don't think I even have the energy left in my body to feel something as heavy as shame right then. 

Mostly, I just feel... well, physically heavy. Just stuffed. My stomach is stretched out, my feet are still throbbing from the concrete floors, and my brain is just kind of buzzing like static. I'll look at the empty containers, and maybe I feel a little, I don't know, annoyed with myself? Like, "Well, that was stupid, Santiago, now you have to go buy more groceries this weekend." But it's not this deep, dark guilt. 

I just take the empty Tupperware—you know, the plastic ones that always get those orange grease stains from the pozole that never really wash out no matter how hard you scrub them with the sponge—and I toss them in the sink. Then I finally unlace my work boots, peel off my socks, and go take my shower. Honestly, the hot water is usually the only thing I'm looking forward to all afternoon anyway. 

So, yeah, I wouldn't say I feel ashamed in that specific moment. I haven't really noticed feeling that way right after my shift. It's more just... being full, and being tired, and just wanting to finally get off my feet and turn my brain off for the night.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences binge eating episodes during the day that are accompanied by feelings of guilt or shame
doctor.question: Do you feel guilty or ashamed after eating a large amount of food during the day, outside of your late-night episodes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling guilty or ashamed after eating (which corresponds to the symptom of feeling disgusted, depressed, or guilty after overeating). This symptom is not present in my profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. Because, see, during the actual day... I don't really eat a large amount of food to begin with. Like I was saying before about my lunch breaks, my day at the warehouse is just so completely scheduled out. From the minute I clock in at 5:30 AM, it's just go, go, go. 

We get exactly thirty minutes for lunch at noon, and they are strict about it. And honestly, doc, by the time you walk all the way from the loading dock—which is way down at the south end of the building—and wait in line at the wash station to scrub the dirt and cardboard dust off your hands with that gritty orange pumice soap they keep in the dispensers... you're left with maybe twenty minutes to actually sit down. 

So I just sit at this wobbly folding table in the breakroom with a couple of the other guys, usually Hector and Dave, and I just eat my regular turkey sandwich or whatever small thing I brought. There's just no opportunity to eat a huge amount of food. You couldn't even if you wanted to, because the foreman is always walking by with his clipboard, tapping his watch and making sure nobody is lingering when the buzzer goes off. 

Because of all that, I'm just eating a normal, quick meal, so there's absolutely nothing to feel guilty or ashamed about. I don't even have time to think about it, I'm just fueling up so I don't pass out when I get back on the forklift. It's really only when I'm totally alone in my house, with no schedule and no one around, that the eating gets out of hand. But during the daylight hours, outside of the house? No, I don't feel any shame or guilt because I'm just doing what everyone else is doing.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating behavior is related to emotional states
doctor.question: Do you usually eat more when you're feeling stressed, anxious, or upset?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about emotional eating or eating in response to negative affect (stress, anxiety, or being upset), which is not explicitly covered by any of the symptom profiles provided.

patient.answer:
Stressed? Anxious? You know, I've thought about that, because you always hear about people doing that on TV—you know, eating a whole carton of ice cream because they had a bad day or they're crying about something. But for me? No, I really don't think so. I haven't noticed a connection like that at all. 

Because, see, when I'm actually stressed out... like, really stressed? My stomach just completely ties itself up into a tight little knot. Like last month, for example, we had our quarterly inventory audit down at the warehouse. Absolute nightmare. The new handheld barcode scanners they gave us weren't syncing up with the main computer database, we had three entire pallets of industrial solvent that completely vanished from the system, and the regional manager is pacing around the floor with this scowl on his face, just looking for someone to blame. That is stress, doc. My heart was pounding, I was sweating right through my uniform shirt, and I was so anxious about getting written up that I couldn't even look at food. Hector offered me half of his meatball sub because I worked right through my lunch break trying to manually reconcile the shipping manifests, and I just waved him off. The thought of eating when I'm worked up like that actually makes me feel a little nauseous. I just drink that terrible breakroom coffee—the stuff that's been sitting on the burner since 6 AM and tastes like burnt pennies—and I keep my head down.

And even if it's not work, like if I'm upset about something personal? Say my ex-wife calls and starts getting on my case about helping pay for our daughter's car repairs, and we get into a whole shouting match over the phone. When I finally hang up, I'm furious, sure. I'm pacing the living room, my blood is boiling. But I don't go straight to the fridge. I'll go out to the garage, maybe organize my socket wrenches, or just sit out on the back porch in the dark and try to cool off. 

The times when I do end up eating all that food late at night... I'm not really upset or anxious when it happens. It's just quiet. The house is totally silent, the TV is usually off. I'm not mad at anyone, I'm not worried about the forklift breaking down, I'm just... there. So, no, I wouldn't say stress or feeling upset is what triggers the eating. If anything, being stressed makes me skip eating entirely.

doctor.question: Do these episodes of eating large amounts of food happen regularly, like on a weekly basis?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: For the past several months, it’s been happening most weeks at least once, usually on a night when there are plenty of leftovers and everyone else has gone to bed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the frequency of the binge eating episodes, specifically if they happen on a weekly basis, which corresponds to the additional requirement for the diagnosis.

patient.answer:
Regularly? Yeah, I suppose it is pretty regular if you look at it on a calendar. I mean, I never really kept a log of it or anything, but... yeah, if I sit down and really think about it, for the past several months, it’s been happening most weeks at least once. 

It kind of started getting into this pattern a while back, maybe around the time the weather started turning and we started getting slammed at the warehouse with the seasonal shipments. You just get into this exhausting rut, you know? But yeah, at least once a week, for sure. 

And it’s almost always on a night when there are plenty of leftovers just sitting right there in the fridge. Like, for instance, on a Sunday I might decide to cook up a massive pot of chili or a huge tray of chicken enchiladas. I do that because I figure, hey, I can pack this up in my cooler and take it to work for lunch all week. It makes sense, right? It saves money, keeps me away from the overpriced vending machines in the breakroom. So I'll have all these containers stacked up on the middle shelf of the fridge, just waiting there. 

But then... well, then a Tuesday or Wednesday night rolls around. And it always happens late. It's usually on a night when everyone else has gone to bed. Like if my daughter is staying over for the week, or if my brother is crashing in the spare room while he looks for a new apartment. Once they finally turn in and shut their doors, the whole house just gets incredibly still. The TV is off, the street outside is quiet, and it feels exactly like I was saying before—like I'm completely alone in the house with no one around. 

It's just me awake in the dark, and I know all that food is just sitting in there, and... I don't know, I just end up eating it. But yeah, to answer your question, it's definitely been a weekly thing for the last few months now.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating episodes are a result of emotional triggers
doctor.question: Do you think your late-night eating episodes are triggered by any specific emotions, such as boredom, sadness, or loneliness?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the late-night eating episodes are triggered by specific emotions such as boredom, sadness, or loneliness, which is not covered by any specific symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Boredom, sadness, loneliness... you know, I've really tried to put my finger on exactly what's going through my head when I'm standing there in front of the open fridge, but honestly? I don't really think it's any of those things. 

Take sadness, for example. I know what sadness feels like. When my dad passed away back in '14, or when the divorce was finalizing and I had to pack up half my life into those cardboard U-Haul boxes while my ex-wife watched from the kitchen... that was sadness. I felt heavy, you know? Like I couldn't get out of bed. But when I'm up at 1 AM eating cold chili out of a Tupperware container, I'm not sad. I'm not crying or feeling sorry for myself at all. 

And loneliness... I mean, sure, like I was saying before, the house is completely empty, or everyone's asleep and their doors are shut. But I've always been a bit of a night owl, ever since I was a kid, really. I actually kind of like the quiet after a long day at the warehouse with all the forklifts beeping and the radios blaring. I don't feel lonely when I'm the only one awake. I'm just... awake. 

As for boredom, well, if you saw my house, you'd know I have a list of chores a mile long. If I was just bored, I could go out to the garage and finish sanding down that old oak coffee table I found at the flea market last month. I've got a whole stack of sandpaper out there—120 grit, 220 grit—just sitting on the workbench waiting for me to get to it. Or I could turn on the TV and watch one of those World War II documentaries on the History Channel. I've got a whole backlog of them recorded on the DVR. So it's not like I don't have plenty of things I could be doing to occupy my time if I was just looking for entertainment. 

It's more just like... my brain just kind of goes completely blank. I'm not trying to fix a bad mood or fill some emotional void or anything dramatic like you see in the movies. I'm not feeling much of anything at all. I just sort of wander into the kitchen, the light from the fridge comes on, and... I don't know, it just happens. There really aren't any big feelings attached to it, if that makes any sense.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating episodes are a result of a lack of control or a deliberate choice
doctor.question: Do you think you would be able to stop eating once you start if you really wanted to?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: What worries me is that once I start picking at the food late at night, I tell myself, 'That's enough, Santiago,' but my hand keeps going back like I don't get to make the decision anymore.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks if the patient feels they can stop eating once they start, which assesses the sense of lack of control over eating during an episode.

patient.answer:
Stop? Man, that’s... that’s the million-dollar question, isn’t it? Because you’d think so. You’d think a grown man, 48 years old, who manages an entire warehouse floor and keeps track of thousands of SKUs every single day, could just put a lid back on a piece of plastic Tupperware and walk away. I mean, it sounds so simple when you say it out loud. Just stop eating. Just close the fridge door. 

But... and this is the part that actually worries me, to be completely honest with you. What worries me is that once I start picking at the food late at night, I literally have this whole conversation with myself in my head. I’ll be standing there in the kitchen, just the light from the refrigerator shining on me, and I’ll look down and see that I’ve already eaten half of my lunches for the rest of the week, and I tell myself, "That's enough, Santiago. Put the fork down. Snap the lid back on and go to bed." I say it just like that, clear as day. 

But then... it’s the strangest thing, doc. My hand just keeps going back. It’s like my arm has a mind of its own, just scooping up another bite, and then another bite, even while my brain is actively telling me to quit. It honestly feels like I don't get to make the decision anymore. 

I’ll even try to physically step back from the counter, you know? Like, I'll take a step back onto the linoleum, wipe my mouth, maybe turn to go rinse the fork off in the sink. But before the water even gets warm, I’m turning right back around to the fridge. It makes absolutely no sense. I want to stop, I really do, because I know I’m gonna be so annoyed the next day when I have to go buy a twelve-dollar turkey sandwich at the deli next to the warehouse because I ate all my meal prep. But in that exact moment, at one or two in the morning... no. I really don't think I can stop. It’s just... the hand keeps moving, no matter what I tell myself.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating episodes are related to a loss of control
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you start, even if you want to?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: What worries me is that once I start picking at the food late at night, I tell myself, 'That's enough, Santiago,' but my hand keeps going back like I don't get to make the decision anymore.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the inability to stop eating once started, which directly corresponds to a loss of control during the eating episode.

patient.answer:
Yeah, exactly. Like I was just saying a second ago, that's really the crux of it. I know I kind of just went on a whole tangent about it, but... yeah, it's exactly that. I am just unable to stop. 

And I want to make sure I'm explaining it right, because honestly, what worries me is that once I start picking at the food late at night, I am fully aware of what's happening. It's not like I'm sleepwalking or in some kind of trance. I literally tell myself, right there in my own head, "That's enough, Santiago. You've had enough, wrap it up." I try to reason with myself the exact same way I'd reason with one of the new forklift drivers on the loading dock who's rushing and messing up a pallet stack. I give myself a direct order to just walk away. 

But... my hand just keeps going back. It keeps scooping up another bite, and then another. It’s like my hand and my brain are completely disconnected from each other. I’ll be staring right at the container, knowing I need that food for my shift tomorrow, knowing I'm going to be mad at myself in the morning, but the fork just keeps moving. 

It really does feel like I don't get to make the decision anymore. It’s a total loss of the steering wheel, you know? Like the brakes are just completely gone. I want to stop, I'm actively telling myself to stop, but the physical action just overrides everything else. It's incredibly frustrating, doc, it really is, because I've always prided myself on being a disciplined guy with my inventory logs and my work schedule, but standing there at the counter... I just can't stop.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating episodes are related to emotional states
doctor.question: Do you think your eating episodes are ever triggered by feelings of emptiness or emotional numbness?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about emotional triggers (emptiness or numbness) for the binge eating episodes, which is not covered by any specific symptom in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Emptiness? Emotional numbness? Hmm. You know, when you use words like that, it makes it sound like... like I'm walking around with this big, gaping hole in my chest, or like I'm totally checked out of my own life. And I really don't think that's it at all. 

I mean, take the warehouse, for example. When we have an empty bay on the floor—say, aisle four, section B—and there are no pallets there... it's just empty. It's just space waiting for the next shipment of auto parts or whatever we're unloading from the trucks that week. It's not a bad thing, it's just a fact of the inventory. But when people talk about emotional emptiness, it always sounds so heavy, you know? Like you're missing a piece of your soul or something dramatic. I don't feel like that. I really don't. I have a good life. I've got a job that keeps me on my toes, I've got guys on the floor who rely on me to make sure the shift runs smooth, I pay my bills on time. I don't feel empty inside. 

And numbness... I mean, what does that even mean, really? Like when you go to the dentist and they shoot your gums full of Novocain to fill a cavity, and you can't feel your own lip for four hours? Or do you mean numb like I just don't care about anything? Because I definitely care. I care a lot. If one of my forklift drivers comes in late, I care. If the inventory logs don't match the physical count at the end of the month, I care—probably too much, honestly, I'll spend three hours tracking down a single missing barcode just to make sure the books are perfect. I'm definitely not walking around like a zombie.

So, no, I wouldn't say I feel numb, and I wouldn't say I feel empty. When I'm standing there in the kitchen at two in the morning... I know I said earlier that my brain goes blank, but it's not because I'm emotionally numb. It's not like I'm trying to stuff food into some deep emotional void to make myself feel alive again. It's just... I'm just standing there, and the eating just starts. I'm not trying to fix anything or run away from any deep, dark feelings of emptiness. I know it probably makes your job harder that I don't have some big psychological reason for it, like you'd read about in a textbook, but I really just don't see it being about feeling empty. It's just me, the fridge, and a complete lack of brakes.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating episodes are related to a lack of control over eating in general
doctor.question: Do you feel like you have control over what you eat during regular meals?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's sense of control during regular meals, whereas the symptom profile only covers loss of control during the binge eating episodes (S050).

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. Regular meals? I have total control. It's actually a night and day difference, doc. 

Like, take my mornings, for example. I'm up at 5:15 AM every single day without fail. I make my coffee—black, no sugar, because I don't want to deal with a sugar crash later when I'm trying to reconcile the shipping manifests—and I make exactly two eggs. Maybe one piece of whole wheat toast. I sit at my little kitchen table, I eat my breakfast, I wash the plate, put it in the drying rack, and I head out the door. It's completely routine. I never sit there feeling like I need to scramble a third egg, or like I'm going to suddenly eat the entire loaf of bread. I just eat what I made, and I'm good.

And then at work, it's the exact same story. We have our lunch whistle at 12:30 PM. Usually, I'll check the loading dock first, just to make sure the afternoon delivery trucks are lined up right, because if I don't keep an eye on them, the new drivers will back in crooked and block bay three. But after I sort that out, I head into the break room, I open up my cooler, and I take out whatever meal prep I brought for the day. Chicken, rice, some green beans, whatever it is. I sit with the guys, we talk about the football game or complain about the regional manager, I finish my Tupperware, and that's it. I'm done. I don't go hunting for quarters for the vending machine, I don't go poking around the communal fridge to see if somebody left a donut in there. I just pack up my bag, wash my fork, and go right back out to the floor. 

Even dinner is usually totally fine. I get home around six, I'm tired, my feet ache from standing on concrete all day, so I'll cook up a pork chop or heat up some soup, sit in my recliner, watch a little TV, and that's that. 

During the day, from 5 AM until maybe 9 or 10 at night, I am completely in the driver's seat. I decide what goes on the plate, I eat it, and I move on with my life. There's no weird pull, no fighting with myself. I plan it out and I execute it, just like I manage the warehouse inventory. So yeah, when it comes to normal, regular meals, I have zero problems. I'm completely in control. That's why the late-night stuff makes me so mad, because I know I have the discipline during the day! It just all goes out the window later on.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition is more aligned with Other Eating Disorders or Binge Eating Disorder
doctor.question: Do you ever eat until you feel uncomfortably full during these episodes?

target_item.name: Eating_Until_Uncomfortably_Full
target_item.manifestation: By the time I finally stop, my stomach feels tight and heavy, and I have to sit on the edge of the couch for a while because bending over or lying down feels bad.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks if the patient eats until feeling uncomfortably full, which matches this symptom.

patient.answer:
Uncomfortably full... yeah. Yeah, that's putting it mildly, doc. It’s like... well, you know when you’re loading a pallet and you try to squeeze just one more row of boxes on top, even though the shrink wrap is already stretching to its absolute limit? That’s what it feels like. 

By the time I finally snap out of it and actually stop eating, my stomach just feels so incredibly tight. Tight and heavy, like I swallowed a cinder block. It's not just the "oh, I had a big Thanksgiving dinner" kind of full where you want to take a nice nap. It's a genuinely bad physical feeling. I'll put whatever container is left in the sink—or the trash, if I finished the whole thing, which happens more often than I want to admit—and I can't even walk straight back to my bedroom. 

I end up having to go into the living room and just sit on the edge of the couch for a while. I can't lean back, I can't bend over... like, if I dropped the TV remote, I couldn't even bend over to pick it up because bending over just feels so bad. And lying down? Forget about it. Lying down is completely out of the question because it makes the pressure so much worse, like all that heavy food is pushing right up into my chest. 

So I just sit there on the very edge of the cushions, kind of staring at the floor, waiting for it to settle down enough so I can finally go lay in bed. And sitting there, in the quiet, feeling like my stomach is about to split open... that's when it really hits me how much I messed up. Because I know I have to be up at 5:15, like I told you, and I'm sitting there at 2:30 in the morning, physically miserable, just waiting for gravity to do its job so I don't feel sick when I lay flat. It's a terrible routine, it really is. It just ruins the whole next morning because I wake up still feeling sluggish and heavy from it all, before I even step foot on the warehouse floor.
